keep: The idea is named up front: watch how far a cell has moved from its own first reading, flag a steady climb, and let a capacity test decide; the sources agree on the habit but not the threshold.

One picture carries the lesson: a 24-cell string's quarterly impedance, a tapped cell's own-baseline line, three readouts (rise from baseline, fitted slope over 4 readings, SDs from the string's mean), a threshold picker, a capacity-test clock against the 80% line, and a charging-history cut-away of four faults.

Worked numbers from the rule: 0.10 / 0.50 = 20% at quarter 15; 5 SDs from the mean; the lines at 0.60, 0.65 to 0.75 and 0.75 mOhm reached at quarters 15, 18 and 23; 7.8 of 10 hours = 78%; 8.5 of 10 = 85%; 0.06 / 0.02 = 3 SDs; the practice cell 0.08 / 0.40 = 20% and 7.5 of 10 = 75%.

Each named slip has a DO screen with a hint per wrong pick: the highest reading as the bad cell (2), the rise taken as the new share or in mOhm (4), a threshold as a verdict (6), lost capacity read as a fail (8), the wrong fault for the history (10), the string mean hiding even ageing (12), a far reading as a verdict (13), equalising a dried-out sealed cell (14). Screen 0 is the Statistics lesson 4 recall opener with 'Still there'.
The disagreement is taught as one: three lines, drawn one at a time, with the 80% capacity line as the shared rule; confidence 'simplified' with one sentence on who argues.

Nine new sources (BU-905 coin toss, the ten-or-eleven trend, BU-804c stratification and equalising, BU-804b crystals, BU-804a shedding, BU-201 reversible versus permanent and dry-out, the acceptance capacity test) were checked by tools/eval/sources.mjs and appended to research.json.
Validator: ok, no problems. Every SHOW screen is under 90 words.
fix: Causal step skipped: why a failing cell's impedance rises at all. Add a 'One way to picture it' line: each fault takes plate or acid out of the work, so the current has less to pass through.
False absolute: 'Real cells all creep upward'. Say real cells tend to creep upward a little with age.
False absolute in the opener: 'A cell rarely fails all at once' is unsourced. Say a cell that is wearing out often shows it slowly.
A footnote on the wrong words: [^12] supports the cause of stratification, not the acid sinking. Say the cell stratifies, as in lesson 2, and leave the sinking to the picture.
Too many footnotes for Dan's 'a few a lesson': drop the separate 'nothing else measures capacity' sentence and the shedding footnote, carry corrosion on [^8], and drop the repeat of [^8] in practice.
Term: 'dries out' is marked as the term; the name is dry-out. Mark [[dry-out]] once, and name the z-score once beside SDs.

shape.ruleInWords: yes: rise = (reading − baseline) ÷ baseline; the slope says how fast; SDs from the mean say how odd; a crossing flags, the capacity test (hours run ÷ rated hours) decides against 80%
shape.workedExampleWithRealNumbers: yes (cell 17: 0.60 mOhm, 20%, 5 SDs, 7.8 h = 78%; practice cell 0.40 to 0.48 mOhm, 20%, 7.5 h = 75%)
shape.misconceptionShownFailing: yes: the highest reading (2), the threshold as a verdict (6), the string mean hiding even ageing (12), equalising a dried-out cell (14)
shape.analogyWithBreaks: yes: trending a motor's insulation resistance against its own history; breaks because IR falls while impedance rises, and IR is the failing property itself while impedance only hints at capacity
shape.practice: yes: steps, rule of thumb, worked example, common mistakes
